title: Why rereading your notes isn't revision
caption: Rereading feels productive. It mostly isn't. Here's what to do instead (and why your brain lies to you about it) 🧠

slides.headline: Rereading your notes {isn't revision}
slides.sub: It feels productive. The research disagrees.

slides.headline: Everyone {does it}
slides.body: In a survey of US university students, rereading notes or textbooks was the most-reported study strategy.

slides.headline: Rated {low utility}
slides.body: A review of 10 study techniques rated rereading “low utility”. Practice testing was rated high.

slides.headline: Why it {fools you}
slides.body: In one study, rereaders felt more confident. But students who tested themselves remembered more a week later.

slides.headline: Do this instead: {blurt}
slides.body: Close the book. Write everything you remember. Then check what you missed. The gaps are your revision.

slides.headline: Questions, {not pages}
slides.body: Turn every heading into a question and answer it from memory. Better still: real past-paper questions.

slides.headline: Test yourself on {real questions}
slides.body: Answer real past-paper questions on Plasmo and get written feedback on every answer.

slides.headline: Save this
slides.small: Send it to the friend still highlighting everything.

sources.title: Metacognitive strategies in student learning: Do students practise retrieval when they study on their own? (Memory 17(4), 471–479)
sources.claim: On an open-ended survey, college students most frequently reported rereading notes or textbook; self-testing ranked low.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques – press summary
sources.claim: Rereading received a low utility rating; practice testing and distributed practice received high utility.

sources.title: Test-Enhanced Learning – APS Observer summary
sources.claim: Repeated studying increased students' confidence, but prior testing produced substantially greater retention on 2-day and 1-week delayed tests.

sources.title: Plasmo – past papers, marked by AI
sources.claim: Real past papers answered online and marked straight away, with written feedback on every answer.
